study_identification.title: Normative Modeling of Thalamic Nuclear Volumes and Characterization of Lateralized Volume Alterations in Alzheimer's Disease Versus Schizophrenia

study_characteristics.study_objective: To establish novel normative models of thalamic nuclear volumes and their laterality indices from a large multi-cohort healthy control sample (n=2374, ages 5-100 years), and to apply these models to investigate shared and distinct volumetric changes in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and schizophrenia (SCZ), linking individual-level deviations to clinical descriptors.

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: Multivariate GAMLSS models: site modeled as random effect (random intercepts via the 'random' function in gamlss R package). OLS and MFP multivariate models: site as fixed effect covariate. Univariate models: ComBat harmonization (NeuroHarmonize Python library, Johnson et al. 2007 empirical Bayes) applied to sex-stratified datasets after eTIV adjustment; site effects first estimated on control samples, then harmonization applied to both cases and controls. ADNI: treated as a single site due to harmonized 3T Siemens acquisition protocol across 44 physical scanners (validated by HIPS-THOMAS showing greater between-scanner than within-scanner variation, Vidal et al. 2024). Covariate analysis showed that site had the smallest individual effect on model performance among age, sex, eTIV, and site.
site_effect_handling_detail.reason: Site effect handling is described in extensive detail across the main methods and supplement. The GAMLSS random effects formulation, OLS/MFP fixed effects, and ComBat harmonization procedure (including the strategy to estimate on controls only) are explicitly stated. The special handling of ADNI as a single site is justified with reference to recent validation work. The relative contribution of site to model performance is quantified in the supplement.
site_effect_handling_detail.supporting_text: site was included as a covariate in multivariate models and modeled as a fixed effect in OLS and MFP models and as a random effect in GAMLSS... volumes were harmonized across sites in sex stratified datasets using ComBat as implemented in Neuroharmonize python library... To reduce the possibility of removing variation related to disease state rather than site, site effects were first estimated using control subjects and harmonization was then applied to both cases and controls... Since the acquisition protocol was harmonized across Siemens 3T scanners, we could treat ADNI as a single site... Recent analyses by Vidal et al. using the Frequently Traveling Human Phantom MRI dataset demonstrated that variation in HIPS-THOMAS segmentation is much higher between scanners than within scanners... Adjusting for eTIV had the largest individual effect on model performance followed by sex while site had the smallest individual effect...

modeling_method.answer: GAMLSS (Generalized Additive Models for Location, Scale and Shape)
modeling_method.reason: Six models were systematically compared (OLS univariate/multivariate, MFP univariate/multivariate, GAMLSS univariate/multivariate) using 5-fold cross-validation across 22 regions (660 trained models total). GAMLSS models showed the best overall performance based on mean absolute error (MAE) and were selected as the top-performing approach. GAMLSS models the mean (μ), standard deviation (σ), skewness (ν), and kurtosis (τ) using the sinh-arcsinh (SHASH) distribution.

deviation_metric.answer: z-scores calculated from normative model residuals: z = (observed volume − fitted μ) / fitted σ (for GAMLSS); Extreme deviations defined as |z| > 1.96 (outside 95th percentile); Infranormal (z < −1.96) and supranormal (z > 1.96) deviations counted per region and per individual; Laterality Index (LI) z-scores for asymmetry analysis; z-score distribution shifts (difference in means) between cases and controls tested with z-test and FDR correction (Benjamini-Hochberg); Regional overlap: percentage of individuals per phenotype with extreme deviation in each region; Centile curves for age-volume trajectories.
deviation_metric.reason: The deviation metrics are explicitly defined in the Methods and Results. z-score calculation formula, threshold for extreme deviations, statistical tests for distribution comparisons, and supplemental overlap/count analyses are all detailed.
deviation_metric.supporting_text: z Scores were calculated for cases and controls from the residuals of fitted values and the standard deviation of residuals in the control samples. In the case of GAMLSS, fitted values were predicted for both μ and σ for each observation. z Scores were then calculated as follows: [formula]... Extreme z-score deviations (infranormal and supranormal) were calculated as those outside the 95th percentile (|z| > 1.96). Regional overlap was calculated for each phenotype as the percentage of participants within each phenotype with an extreme z-score deviation in each region... z-Score distributions in cases and controls were compared with the z test for each region. To control for multiple testing, p values were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg method, and a false discovery rate threshold of false discovery rate-adjusted p < .05 was set.

clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed:
Answer: Alzheimer's disease: Clear progression of thalamic nuclear involvement from EMCI through LMCI to AD. Extreme deviations in controls: 42.4% infranormal, 48.4% supranormal. EMCI: 52.1% infranormal, 52.6% supranormal; LMCI: 67.3% infranormal, 43.4% supranormal; AD: 82.8% infranormal, 33.3% supranormal (Supplemental Table 10). Bilateral AV, MD/Pf, and Pul nuclei most severely affected across all AD/MCI stages. Left AV nucleus shows largest effect in AD and is the most affected nucleus in each cohort. Greater z-score shifts on the left than right in whole thalamus and MD/Pf. Laterality Index differences in EMCI: whole thalamus, VLp (smaller left volumes), MGN (smaller right volume). Most regions show weak to moderate correlations with MMSE (r=0.11-0.34) and MoCA (r=0.12-0.32); bilateral thalamus, AV, Pul, MD/Pf show strongest correlations with MMSE, MoCA, and amyloid-tau index (ATI). Schizophrenia: Heterogeneous patterns across subgroups. All SCZ (n=168): 13 of 20 thalamic regions show significant z-score shifts (11 nuclei + bilateral whole thalamus); right AV, VA, VLa unique to right side; bilateral Pul, MD/Pf, CM affected. Laterality Index shifts: whole thalamus, VA, VLp, MGN (smaller right volumes). Early SCZ (n=83): subset of All SCZ findings; left whole thalamus and Pul more affected than right; Pul and VPL Laterality Index indicates left < right volumes. UCLA SCZ (n=41): no significant z-score shifts, but moderate inverse correlations with SAPS/SANS global ratings predominantly in left thalamic regions (left VA r=−0.65 with Global Positive Thought Disorder, FDR-adjusted p=0.00056). SCZ +AH (n=21): most findings on right side; largest shifts in right MGN, right Pul, bilateral MD/Pf, right whole thalamus; Laterality Index indicates smaller right volumes in multiple nuclei; right MD/Pf associated with disorganized thought severity (r=−0.53, p=0.012) and persistent auditory hallucinations. SCZ −AH (n=23): most significant shifts on right; all Laterality Index shifts indicate smaller right volumes. Regional overlap: EMCI 49.4% infranormal, 34.9% supranormal; UCLA SCZ 41.5%/41.5%; SCZ −AH 65.2%/52.2%; SCZ +AH 61.9%/42.9%. Normative modeling identified more significant thalamic regions than conventional case-control analysis (e.g., All SCZ 13 vs 12; Early SCZ 9 vs 2; EMCI 10 vs 7; AD 18 vs 17; Supplemental Table 4). AD vs SCZ comparison: Bilateral Pul and MD/Pf affected in both, but significantly larger effect in AD. Largest difference: left AV nucleus (severely affected in AD, not significant in any SCZ cohort). All SCZ appears between EMCI and LMCI in severity for some regions (right VA, right VLp). Model performance: GAMLSS multivariate mean test MAE 56.51 mm³ (train 55.68 mm³); no significant train-test difference (p≥0.93). eTIV had largest effect on model performance, followed by sex, then age, then site (Supplemental Figure 2). Centile plots show differential age associations: linear trends in whole thalamus, Pul, AV, MGN; peak around age 30-40 then decline in CM, VLa, VPL, LGN (Figure 2, Supplemental Figure 3).

clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations:
Answer: Moderate normative reference sample size (n=2374, adequate per Ge et al. but smaller than some recent efforts); relatively small SCZ cohort sizes (particularly SCZ +AH n=21, SCZ −AH n=23, UCLA SCZ n=41); absence of some thalamic nuclei (e.g., centrolateral, intralaminar nuclei) from segmentation/analysis; same GAMLSS model structure applied across all regions rather than region-specific optimization; small nuclei (LGN, MGN) more susceptible to subtle variability and imaging artifacts despite accurate segmentation; relevant potential confounders not addressed in current analysis: disease duration, substance abuse, medication burden, head motion; interpretation of volumetric changes assumes volume loss reflects network dysfunction without direct assessment of structural/functional connectivity; reliance on cross-sectional data rather than longitudinal trajectories.
Confidence Rating: High
Negative Answer Category: Not Negative
Reason: Limitations are explicitly discussed in a dedicated paragraph near the end of the Discussion section.
Supporting Text: Weaknesses of the current study include a relatively small number of individuals in the SCZ cohorts, a moderate sample size for normative modeling, absence of some thalamic nuclei such as the centrolateral or intralaminar nuclei in the analyses, and using the same model for all regions. Additionally, our AD analyses suggest that our model performed well even in the older age ranges, and previous analyses by Ge et al. suggest that a sample size of 2000 to 3000 is adequate to optimize a normative model's performance. Our interpretation of volumetric changes is dependent on a change in volume being associated with a change in network function without assessing the network directly... Some regions such as the LGN and MGN are small and potentially more susceptible to subtle variability and imaging artifacts despite their accurate segmentation. Results concerning these nuclei should be interpreted with caution. Finally, relevant factors such as disease duration, substance abuse, medication burden, and head motion that may confound results were outside the scope of these analyses.

clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes:
Answer: First normative models of thalamic nuclear laterality indices (LI), enabling novel characterization of left-right asymmetry deviations. Systematic comparison of three modeling approaches (OLS, MFP, GAMLSS) with univariate/multivariate variants (6 models total, 660 trained models across regions), providing methodological guidance for future normative modeling. Combined site effect handling strategies (ComBat batch removal for univariate models; hierarchical random effects in GAMLSS multivariate models) with explicit comparison of effectiveness. HIPS-THOMAS segmentation method on standard clinical T1 MRI (not requiring specialized sequences), increasing accessibility and enabling retrospective analysis of existing datasets. Centile curves across full lifespan (ages 5-100) revealing distinct age-volume trajectories per nucleus (some linear, others peak in midlife then decline). Comparison to traditional case-control analysis demonstrates increased sensitivity of normative modeling (more significant regions detected, especially in early disease stages and heterogeneous disorders like SCZ). Multi-cohort design spanning development, young adulthood, and aging enhances generalizability. Models and code publicly available (https://github.com/thalamicseg/hipsthomasdocker). Conservative QC approach (6×IQR outlier threshold, visual inspection, reprocessing/exclusion of failed segmentations) enhances reference sample quality. Application validates models by showing expected AD progression (EMCI < LMCI < AD) and correlation patterns with established biomarkers (MMSE, MoCA, amyloid-tau index), supporting clinical validity. Novel neuroanatomical insights: right MD/Pf as potential key mediator of multiple SCZ symptoms (thought disorder, hallucinations), affected early in disease course; asymmetric patterns (left-sided in early MCI, right-sided in SCZ) suggest differential pathophysiological mechanisms.
Confidence Rating: High
Negative Answer Category: Not Negative
Reason: Multiple novel methodological and clinical contributions are highlighted throughout the manuscript, particularly in the Abstract, Discussion, and Conclusions.
Supporting Text: To the best of our knowledge, we present the first normative models of LI... our centile curves provide important insight into volume changes to thalamic nuclear regions across the lifespan, about which there is a paucity of research... There was an increase in the number of statistically significant thalamic regions identified using normative modeling... Normative models, HIPS-THOMAS, and R code are available at: https://github.com/thalamicseg/hipsthomasdocker... We observed a predilection for right thalamic regions in all but one of the SCZ cohorts... We found that the right MD/Pf region was associated with severity of formal thought disorder ratings and persistent auditory verbal hallucinations... The MD nucleus... allows it to regulate and coordinate multifaceted networks relevant to language, motivated behavior, attention and horizontal gaze, emotion, and executive function and working memory... the right MD nucleus was affected early in the course of SCZ whereas the left MD nucleus was not affected... Taken together, this suggests a key role for the right MD nucleus in the development of multiple facets of SCZ through dysregulated network activity.

general_notes.general_notes: Total participants screened: 2978. Total passing QC: 2954 (99.2% pass rate; 24 excluded/reprocessed, 0.8%). Final sample: Controls n=2374 (F=1279, 53.9%; M=1095, 46.1%), Cases n=580 (F=244, M=336). Control age range: 5.6-100 years (overall mean/SD not reported; cohort-specific means/SDs available in Table 2). ADNI special handling: 44 physical sites aggregated as single site due to harmonized 3T Siemens acquisition protocol; justified by HIPS-THOMAS validation showing within-scanner variation < between-scanner variation (Vidal et al. 2024). MRI acquisition parameters per cohort detailed in Supplementary Table 7 (vendors: Siemens, Philips; field strength: all 3T; sequences: MPRAGE, ME-MPRAGE, 3DFFE; voxel sizes: 0.7-1.2mm). Segmentation includes 22 regions total: 2 whole thalami + 20 individual nuclei (10 bilateral). Two additional extrathalamic structures segmented but not analyzed: habenula, mammillothalamic tract. Training times (left whole thalamus, 20 iterations, Apple M1 Max): GAMLSS multivariate ~14.4s, GAMLSS univariate ~5.9s, MFP multivariate ~0.21s, MFP univariate ~0.04s, OLS multivariate ~0.003s, OLS univariate ~0.001s (Supplemental Table 9). Normative models trained independently per region (22 separate models). Preprint: medRxiv doi:10.1101/2024.03.06.24303871. Funding: NIBIB R01EB032674 (MS). Data sources: HCP (1U54MH091657), HCP-Development (U01MH109589), HCP-Aging (U01AG052564), HCP-EP (U01MH109977), ADNI (U01 AG024904, W81XWH-12-2-0012), OpenNeuro ds000030 (UCLA), OpenNeuro ds004302 (SCZ AH). Control cohorts by site: HCP DEV (4 sites: Harvard n=206, UCLA n=124, UMinn n=154, WashU n=141); HCP YA (1 site: WashU n=719, note: sibling pairs included); HCP AGE (4 sites: MGH n=159, UCLA n=140, UMinn n=197, WashU n=201); HCP EP (4 sites: BWH controls n=8, IU controls n=24, MGH controls n=10, McLean controls n=11); UCLA (2 scanners: 35343 controls n=94, 35426 controls n=21); SCZ AH (1 site: controls n=19 per Supplemental Table 6, but n=22 or n=23 per text; discrepancy noted); ADNI (treated as 1 site: controls n=123 per Supplemental Table 6, n=124 per text). Clinical assessments: MMSE (Folstein et al. 1975), MoCA (Nasreddine et al. 2005), amyloid-tau index calculated as Aβ/(240+1.8×tau) per Tariciotti et al. 2018; PSYRATS Auditory Hallucination subscale (Haddock et al. 1999); SAPS/SANS (Andreasen 1989, 1995); PANSS (Kay et al. 1987) with Marder 5-factor structure. Statistical software: R (gamlss, mfp, base lm, microbenchmark packages); Python (NeuroHarmonize); jamovi 2.3.28.0; FreeSurfer mri_segstats. Quality control: Custom Python script for visual QC. z-score distributions for controls approximate normal distributions centered at 0 for all 22 regions and LIs (Figure 3). Within-control asymmetries detected: left AV < right AV (diff=−0.17, p=1.51E-05), left VLa < right VLa (diff=−0.10, p=9.55E-03), left Pul > right Pul (diff=0.08, p=4.62E-02) in healthy controls (Supplemental Table 8), indicating normative asymmetries captured by the models. AD pathology interpretation: Results concordant with known AV-MD-Pul connectivity to medial temporal and medial prefrontal/parietal regions, matching typical amyloid/tau progression and observations of subcortical spread (Bernstein et al. 2021, Aggleton et al. 2016, Busche & Hyman 2020, Cho et al. 2018). SCZ interpretation: Right MD/Pf dysfunction may underlie multiple symptoms via widespread MD connectivity to prefrontal cortex, basal ganglia, amygdala, temporal lobe, anterior cingulate (Schmahmann 2003, Georgescu et al. 2020, Barbas et al. 2013, Pergola et al. 2018). Laterality findings may reflect psychopathology differences (Lubben et al. 2021, Tomer et al. 2013, Tiihonen et al. 1998). Prior thalamic nuclei work: Recent studies (Huang et al. 2024, Mørch-Johnsen et al. 2023, Dönmezler et al. 2024, Thalhammer et al. 2024, Perez-Rando et al. 2022) identified MD, Pul, LGN, MGN, ventrolateral associations in SCZ; current study extends to include right AV, VA, bilateral CM and systematically compares to AD. Study design enables AD-SCZ comparison: Both disorders share some thalamic involvement (bilateral Pul, MD/Pf) but differ markedly in laterality (AD more symmetric, SCZ right-predominant), regional specificity (left AV unique to AD; right AV, VA, VLa unique to SCZ), severity (larger shifts in AD), and progression (clear EMCI-LMCI-AD gradient vs heterogeneous SCZ subgroups). Methodological note: eTIV adjustment reduces model MAE most among covariates, followed by sex, age, site (Supplemental Figure 2), highlighting importance of TIV correction in subcortical volumetric normative modeling.
